title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
seo_title: Year 9 Science: Chemical Reactions and Equations Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Model the rearrangement of atoms in chemical reactions using a range of representations, including word and simple balanced chemical equations, and use these to explain the law of conservation of mass; including combustion and the reactions of acids (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 9 science worksheets on chemical reactions: word and balanced symbol equations, conservation of mass, combustion, acids and bases, pH, neutralisation and reactions of acids with metals and carbonates. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Atoms are rearranged in a reaction, so each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.
body_html:
How to think about it

In a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged into new substances.

  • Word equation: reactants → products. A balanced symbol equation shows the same number of each atom on both sides.
  • Balance by putting numbers in front of formulas; never change the small subscripts.
  • Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen; acid + base → salt + water; acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Example

Balance: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O

2 O on the left

make 2H₂O

then 2H₂

Answer: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

Example

Hydrochloric acid + zinc → ?

acid + metal → salt + hydrogen

Answer: zinc chloride + hydrogen

Common mistakes

  • Changing subscripts (H₂O to H₂O₂) to balance an equation.
  • Thinking pH 7 is acidic (it is neutral).
  • Leaving out carbon dioxide when an acid reacts with a carbonate.

faq.q: How do I balance a chemical equation?
faq.a: Count each type of atom on both sides. Put whole numbers (coefficients) in front of formulas until every element matches. Never change the subscripts.

faq.q: Why does mass seem to change in some reactions?
faq.a: If a gas escapes from an open container or joins from the air, the measured mass changes. In a closed system the total mass stays the same.
It is the reaction of an acid with a base to make a salt and water. Antacids and lime for soil both work by neutralisation.

items.q: Which coefficients (in order) balance this equation? BaCl<sub>2</sub> + Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → BaSO<sub>4</sub> + NaCl
items.e: Check: BaCl<sub>2</sub> + Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → BaSO<sub>4</sub> + 2NaCl.

items.q: How many atoms of Na are in 2NaCl?
items.e: 2NaCl: the coefficient 2 multiplies every atom in the formula, so 2 × 1 = 2.

items.q: When balancing, what may you change?
items.e: Changing subscripts changes the substance.

items.q: How many atoms of H are in 2Al(OH)<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 2Al(OH)<sub>3</sub>: the coefficient 2 multiplies every atom in the formula, so 2 × 3 = 6.

items.q: Which coefficients (in order) balance this equation? N<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → NH<sub>3</sub>
items.e: Check: N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>.

items.q: Which coefficients (in order) balance this equation? P<sub>4</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>
items.e: Check: P<sub>4</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>.

items.q: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
c: Atoms are not created or destroyed, so each side must have the same number of each atom.
items.e: This shows conservation of mass.

items.q: How many atoms of O are in 3O<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: 3O<sub>2</sub>: the coefficient 3 multiplies every atom in the formula, so 3 × 2 = 6.

items.q: How many atoms of Na are in 2Na?
items.e: 2Na: the coefficient 2 multiplies every atom in the formula, so 2 × 1 = 2.

items.q: What is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of methane?
items.e: 1 C, 4 H and 4 O on each side.

items.q: What does the subscript 2 in H₂O mean?
c: two hydrogen atoms in each molecule
items.e: Subscripts are part of the formula.

items.q: In a balanced equation, what must be the same on both sides?
c: the number of atoms of each element
items.e: Atoms, not molecules.

items.q: How many atoms of Cl are in 2KClO<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 2KClO<sub>3</sub>: the coefficient 2 multiplies every atom in the formula, so 2 × 1 = 2.

items.q: What is made when candle wax (a hydrocarbon) burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
items.e: Hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: What is made when hydrogen burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
items.e: Hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: Which coefficients (in order) balance this equation? Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → MgO
items.e: Check: 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO.

items.q: Write the word equation for an acid reacting with a carbonate.
c: acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide
items.e: The fizzing is carbon dioxide.

items.q: How many atoms of O are in 6O<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: 6O<sub>2</sub>: the coefficient 6 multiplies every atom in the formula, so 6 × 2 = 12.

items.q: Farmers in Western Australia spread lime (calcium carbonate) on acidic soils. Why?
c: It neutralises the acid in the soil.
It makes the soil more acidic.
items.e: Soil acidity is a big problem in WA wheat belts.

items.q: Which salt forms when sulfuric acid reacts with magnesium?
items.e: Sulfuric acid makes sulfate salts.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KBr → 2KCl + 3Br<sub>2</sub>
c: No. There are too many arrows.
Yes. Both sides have the same elements.
No. Br has 2 atoms on the left and 6 on the right.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: What number replaces ? to balance the equation? BaCl<sub>2</sub> + Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → BaSO<sub>4</sub> + ?NaCl
items.e: Balanced: BaCl<sub>2</sub> + Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → BaSO<sub>4</sub> + 2NaCl.

items.q: What number replaces ? to balance the equation? Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KBr → ?KCl + Br<sub>2</sub>
items.e: Balanced: Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br<sub>2</sub>.

items.q: What number replaces ? to balance the equation? 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + ?O<sub>2</sub>
items.e: Balanced: 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub>.

items.q: Write the word equation for an acid reacting with a metal.
items.e: Hydrogen 'pops' with a lit splint.

items.q: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, how many oxygen atoms are on each side?
items.e: O₂ has 2; 2MgO has 2.

items.q: Mia reacts 10 g of hydrogen with 80 g of oxygen. Both are used up. What mass of water forms?
items.e: Mass is conserved: 10 + 80 = 90 g.

items.q: What number replaces ? to balance the equation? 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → ?MgO
items.e: Balanced: 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO.

items.q: In Mia's sealed flask, some hydrogen reacts with 40 g of oxygen and makes 45 g of water. What mass of hydrogen reacted?
What number replaces ? to balance the equation? 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → ?H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>
items.e: Balanced: 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>.

items.q: Which salt forms when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
items.e: Hydrochloric acid makes chloride salts.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub> → 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
c: No. There are too many arrows.
Yes. Both sides have the same elements.
No. H has 12 atoms on the left and 6 on the right.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? 4C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
c: No. There are too many arrows.
No. C has 8 atoms on the left and 2 on the right.
Yes. Both sides have the same elements.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: In Mei's sealed flask, some copper reacts with 2 g of sulfur and makes 10 g of copper(I) sulfide. What mass of copper reacted?
Is this equation balanced? 3Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> → Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O
c: Yes. Each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.
No. There are more molecules on the right.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: What number replaces ? to balance the equation? ?Fe + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>
items.e: Balanced: 4Fe + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.

items.q: Ethan heats 75 g of calcium carbonate in an open dish. It leaves 42 g of calcium oxide. What mass of carbon dioxide gas escaped?
items.e: Mass is conserved: 75 − 42 = 33 g of gas.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? 2C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> + 13O<sub>2</sub> → 8CO<sub>2</sub> + 10H<sub>2</sub>O
c: No. There are more molecules on the right.
Yes. Each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? 2Na + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 2NaOH + H<sub>2</sub>
c: Yes. Each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.
No. There are more molecules on the right.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? 2C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> + 13O<sub>2</sub> → 8CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O
c: No. H has 20 atoms on the left and 2 on the right.
Yes. Both sides have the same elements.
No. There are too many arrows.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: What is made when carbon (charcoal) burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
items.e: Hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: What is made when propane burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
items.e: Hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: Which change is NOT allowed when balancing an equation?
c: changing the small numbers (subscripts) in a formula
adding a big number in front of a formula
items.e: Changing H₂O to H₂O₂ makes a different substance.

items.q: Kai tests a gas from acid and zinc with a lit splint. It makes a squeaky pop. What is the gas?
items.e: Oxygen relights a glowing splint; CO₂ turns limewater milky.

items.q: What is made when methane (natural gas) burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
items.e: Hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: Why does a burning candle seem to lose mass?
c: The products (CO₂ and water vapour) escape into the air.
items.e: Open system.

items.q: What is the law of conservation of mass?
c: Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.
items.e: Lavoisier.

items.q: Write the word equation for an acid reacting with a base (neutralisation).
items.e: The products are neutral.

items.q: What is made when sulfur burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
items.e: Hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: What is made when magnesium burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
items.e: Hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: Mia reacts 2.4 g of magnesium with acid in an open flask. The flask loses 0.2 g. Why?
c: Hydrogen gas escaped into the air.
Mass is not conserved in reactions.
items.e: In a closed flask the mass would stay the same.

items.q: Why do people take antacid tablets for heartburn?
c: They are bases that neutralise excess stomach acid.
items.e: Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid.

items.q: Liam burns a candle under a glass jar. The flame goes out. Why?
c: The oxygen in the jar has been used up.
items.e: Combustion needs oxygen.

items.q: What is the first step in balancing an equation?
c: count the atoms of each element on both sides
items.e: Make a tally.

items.q: Tom reacts 70 g of iron with 40 g of sulfur. Both are used up. What mass of iron sulfide forms?
items.e: Mass is conserved: 70 + 40 = 110 g.

items.q: What pH does a neutral solution have?
items.e: Below 7 is acidic; above 7 is basic.

items.q: Noah builds a ball-and-stick model of 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. How many hydrogen balls does he need on each side?
items.e: 2H₂ has 4 hydrogen atoms; 2H₂O has 4.

items.q: Ruby adds marble chips to acid and records the mass every minute. The mass falls quickly, then slowly, then stops. Why does it stop?
c: The acid or marble has been used up, so no more carbon dioxide is made.
items.e: Reactions stop when a reactant runs out.

items.q: Jack adds drops of indicator to vinegar, water and bicarb soda solution. Which will show the highest pH?
items.e: Bicarb soda solution is weakly basic.

items.q: Why must chemical equations be balanced?
c: To make the equation look neat.
Atoms are not created or destroyed in a reaction.
items.e: Conservation of mass.

items.q: Zinc reacts with sulfuric acid. Which gas is produced?
c: hydrogen, which burns with a 'pop' sound
no gas; a salt and water form
oxygen, which relights a glowing splint
carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky
items.e: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Acid + alkali → salt + water.

items.q: Nitric acid reacts with magnesium oxide. Which salt is made?
items.e: Hydrochloric acid → chloride; sulfuric acid → sulfate; nitric acid → nitrate. The metal comes from the alkali or base.

items.q: Nitric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide. Which salt is made?
items.e: Hydrochloric acid → chloride; sulfuric acid → sulfate; nitric acid → nitrate. The metal comes from the alkali or base.

items.q: Sulfuric acid reacts with potassium hydroxide. Which salt is made?
items.e: Hydrochloric acid → chloride; sulfuric acid → sulfate; nitric acid → nitrate. The metal comes from the alkali or base.

items.q: What colour is Universal Indicator in a neutral solution?
items.e: Red to yellow is acidic; blue to purple is alkaline.

items.q: Universal indicator turns orange. What kind of solution is it?
items.e: Red–orange–yellow: acid; green: neutral; blue–purple: alkali.

items.q: Why is Universal Indicator more useful than litmus?
c: It shows how strongly acidic or alkaline a solution is, not just whether it is acidic or alkaline.
items.e: It gives a pH value from its colour.

items.q: What is neutralisation?
c: the breaking down of a substance by heat
the dissolving of salt in water
the reaction of a metal with oxygen
the reaction between an acid and an alkali to form a salt and water
items.e: The pH moves towards 7.

items.q: Hydrochloric acid reacts with copper oxide. Which salt is made?
items.e: Hydrochloric acid → chloride; sulfuric acid → sulfate; nitric acid → nitrate. The metal comes from the alkali or base.

items.q: Sugar solution has a pH of 7. Is it acidic, alkaline or neutral?
items.e: Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline.

items.q: Potassium hydroxide reacts with nitric acid. Which gas is produced?
c: hydrogen, which burns with a 'pop' sound
no gas; a salt and water form
oxygen, which relights a glowing splint
carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky
items.e: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Acid + alkali → salt + water.

items.q: Which is the most acidic? salt solution (pH 7); stomach acid (pH 1); cola drink (pH 3); sodium hydroxide solution (pH 14)
items.e: The lower the pH, the more acidic the solution.

items.q: Universal indicator turns purple. What kind of solution is it?
items.e: Red–orange–yellow: acid; green: neutral; blue–purple: alkali.

items.q: Universal indicator turns yellow. What is the pH?
items.e: Red–orange–yellow: acid; green: neutral; blue–purple: alkali.

items.q: What colour is universal indicator in a solution of pH 7?
items.e: Red–orange–yellow: acid; green: neutral; blue–purple: alkali.

items.q: Complete the word equation: zinc + sulfuric acid → ?
items.e: The salt is named from the metal and the acid.

items.q: Complete the word equation: iron + hydrochloric acid → ?
items.e: The salt is named from the metal and the acid.

items.q: Which is the most alkaline? bleach (pH 12); sodium hydroxide solution (pH 14); vinegar (pH 3); lemon juice (pH 2)
items.e: The higher the pH, the more alkaline the solution.

items.q: Complete the word equation: sodium carbonate + sulfuric acid → ?
items.e: The salt is named from the metal and the acid.

items.q: Nitric acid reacts with calcium hydroxide. Which salt is made?
items.e: Hydrochloric acid → chloride; sulfuric acid → sulfate; nitric acid → nitrate. The metal comes from the alkali or base.

items.q: A sealed bag of bicarb soda and vinegar is weighed before and after reacting. What will the scale show?
items.e: Closed system.

items.q: Why do we use the lowest whole-number coefficients?
c: It is the simplest ratio of the substances.
items.e: 4H₂ + 2O₂ → 4H₂O is the same ratio.

items.q: How could you find the exact amount of alkali needed to neutralise some acid?
c: Pour it all in at once.
Add the alkali slowly, measuring the pH, until it reaches 7.
items.e: Careful method.

items.q: Pure water has a pH of 7. Is it acidic, alkaline or neutral?
items.e: Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline.

items.q: Why is red cabbage water used as an indicator at home?
c: It changes colour in acids and alkalis.
items.e: Natural indicator.

items.q: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution drop by drop to hydrochloric acid with Universal Indicator. How does the colour change?
items.e: The pH rises towards 7.

items.q: Burning steel wool on a balance gets heavier. Why?
c: Oxygen from the air combines with the iron.
items.e: The product includes oxygen atoms.

items.q: A solution turns Universal Indicator purple. What is its likely pH?
items.e: Purple means strongly alkaline.

items.q: Vinegar has a pH of 3. Is it acidic, alkaline or neutral?
items.e: Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline.

items.q: Why should you add acid to water, and not water to concentrated acid?
c: Adding water to concentrated acid can make it spit dangerously.
items.e: Safety.

items.q: Butterfly pea flower tea turns pink when lime juice is added. What does this show?
items.e: Natural indicators change colour with pH.

items.q: A student balances H₂ + O₂ → H₂O by writing H₂O₂. What is wrong?
c: She changed a subscript, which made a different substance (hydrogen peroxide).
items.e: Use 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

items.q: Ella adds sodium hydroxide drop by drop to acid with universal indicator. The colour changes from red to green. What has happened?
items.e: Green means neutral.

items.q: Universal indicator turns red. What is the pH?
items.e: Red–orange–yellow: acid; green: neutral; blue–purple: alkali.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? 2Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> → Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O
c: No. Ca has 2 atoms on the left and 3 on the right.
No. There are too many arrows.
Yes. Both sides have the same elements.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: Marble statues slowly wear away in polluted rain. Why?
c: Marble is an alkali that dissolves in water.
Marble is calcium carbonate, which reacts with acids in the rain.
items.e: Carbon dioxide is given off.

items.q: Universal indicator turns blue. What is the pH?
items.e: Red–orange–yellow: acid; green: neutral; blue–purple: alkali.

items.q: A student says all acids are dangerous. Is that right?
c: No. Weak acids like those in fruit are safe to eat.
items.e: Strength matters.

items.q: How can a model with coloured beads show conservation of mass?
c: The same beads are rearranged into new groups, none added or removed.
items.e: Atoms rearrange.

items.q: Which is the most alkaline? soap solution (pH 9); vinegar (pH 3); sodium hydroxide solution (pH 14); toothpaste (pH 8)
items.e: The higher the pH, the more alkaline the solution.
